newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Clinton inks nuclear treaty, urges wider UN action.
newsitem.headline: Clinton inks nuclear treaty, urges wider UN action.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Tuesday signed a landmark treaty that bans all nuclear testing and called on the global community to get tougher on terrorists and drug traffickers.

Using the 51st session of the U.N. General Assembly to sketch out an election-year vision of international peace and prosperity, Clinton said the countries of the world needed to cooperate against terrorism and illegal drugs because no country was immune from these menaces.
"Last year I asked the nations assembled here to commit to a goal of zero tolerance for aggression, terrorism and lawless behaviour. Frankly, we haven't done that yet.

"Real zero tolerance means giving no aid and no quarter to terrorists who slaughter the innocent and drug traffickers who poison our children and to do everything we can to prevent weapons of mass destruction from falling into the wrong hands," he said.

Illustrating his determination to combat drugs, Clinton said he would provide "more than $100 million worth of defence equipment, services and training" to America's southern neighbours. This could help blunt Republican criticism of Clinton's anti-drug efforts.
The White House said Clinton notified Congress on Sept. 14, and that the money would provide helicopters, patrol boats and other equipment to Mexico, Colombia, Peru, Venezuela and other nations.
Clinton spoke to the U.N. delegates after making the United States the first signatory of the new Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT), which is designed to end all nuclear explosions.
He signed the agreement, which is expected to face a difficult fight for ratification in the U.S. Senate, with the same pen President John Kennedy used to sign a limited test ban treaty in 1963.

"The CTBT is the shared work of hard negotiation. Some have complained that it does not mandate total nuclear disarmament by a date certain," the president said. "I would say to them do not forsake the benefits of this achievement by ignoring the tremendous progress we have already made toward that goal."

That was a veiled message to India, which exploded a nuclear device in 1974 and now vows to block the treaty from taking force. It maintains the pact is flawed because it does not commit the nuclear powers to eventually destroy their arsenals, and in fact lets them develop more sophisticated means of testing without explosions.

Clinton also called for six follow-on arms control measures, including implementation of a chemical weapons treaty, a freeze on the production of nuclear bomb-making material, improving compliance with a biological weapons treaty and a ban on anti-personnel landmines.
In doing so, he took an indirect swipe at Republican rival Bob Dole, who two weeks ago abruptly withdrew his support for the chemical weapons treaty, dooming U.S. ratification this year.

"I deeply regret that the United States Senate has not yet voted on the convention, but I want to assure you and people throughout the world that I will not let this treaty die," Clinton told the delegates.

Clinton's visit to U.N. headquarters was flavored by controversy over his effort to dump Egypt's Boutros Boutros- Ghali as secretary-general of the world body. The two posed for pictures together, but the atmosphere was correct rather than cordial.
Asked by reporters if they discussed Boutros-Ghali's future, Clinton said: "There was nothing to discuss. Our position is clear and it is set, and there's nothing to talk about."

Clinton made no mention of the issue in his speech, saying only that his administration favoured "streamlining the bureaucracy and reining in the budget" of the UN, and that he was committed to paying past-due U.S. financial obligations to the world body.

After his speech, Clinton had separate private meetings with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, Saudi Arabian Foreign Minister Saud al-Faisal and Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primacov. White House spokesman Mike McCurry said the situations in Bosnia and Iraq were addressed at all three meetings.
